## Advanced effort estimation in software projects using ensemble-based fusion techniques

Ritu [a][,][*], Pankaj Bhambri [b], Mudassir Khan [c][,][*], Barga Mohammed Mujahid [d]

a *Department of Computer Science & Engineering, Guru Nanak Dev Engineering College, Ludhiana, Punjab, India and Department of Computer Science & Engineering, I.K.*
*Gujral Punjab Technical University, Jalandhar, Punjab, India*
b *Department of Information Technology, Guru Nanak Dev Engineering College, Ludhiana, Punjab, India*
c *Department of Computer Science, College of Computer Science, Applied College Tanumah, King Khalid University, Abha, Saudi Arabia*

A R T I C L E I N F O

*Keywords:*

**1. Introduction**


A B S T R A C T

The software development process heavily relies on effort estimation, which is crucial for determining the
development approach and methodology. This research aims to propose a methodology to enhance effort esti-­
mation, ensuring that initial work estimation remains precise and reliable. In such cases, a fusion approach using
an ensemble of Machine Learning (ML) techniques is proposed. The proposed methodology uses linear regression
and random forest ML algorithms. The results are cross-checked against well-known datasets to demonstrate
their estimation accuracy. A ML method is used to forecast the project’s effort, as some parameters required for
work estimation may not be determinable at the beginning of the process. The model is trained using parametric
training with fixed-size parameters, with the use case repository data serving as the training set and the China
dataset as the test set. The proposed work uses an ensemble model to compute the fusion approach’s result,
which is then inputted into a linear regression model. All regression models are then run individually to calculate
the effort, and the efficiency of the proposed model is 94% which is a great improvement as compared to the
individual model’s performance which is 74% only.


Effort estimation in Software Engineering refers to the process of
predicting the amount of work (usually measured in person-hours,
person-days, or person-months) required to complete a software devel-­
opment task, Project, or phase. Accurate effort estimation is crucial
because it helps project managers, developers, and stakeholders plan,
allocate resources, set timelines, and manage risks effectively. Estima-­
tion approaches can be categorized into a wide range of groups. The sizecentered estimation approach serves as the foundation for the formal
estimating model's investigations of Function Point Analysis (FPA), Class
Point Analysis (CPA), and Use Case Point Analysis (UCP). The Estima-­
tion Effort, or necessary effort, for completing the SD(software Devel-­
opment) is determined using UCP. The estimation effort for the UCP
approach (UC) is based on the modeling software with use cases.
Multiplying UCP by the Effort Rate (ER) number yields the Estimation
Effort. The ER, which is determined using the previously mentioned
project information, is used to determine the total number of human

 - Corresponding author.


resources needed for a project. The only reason CPA is used in this case is
that the class point is assumed to be a class diagram, which is one of the
most significant Unified Modeling Language (UML) diagrams. The pri-­
mary benefit of utilizing CPA as opposed to FPA is that the class point is
established during the SDLC's design phase, whereas the total FP is
calculated during the coding phase. As a result, estimating can be
completed early in the SDLC. The software Development Efforts Esti-­
mation (SDEE) serves as the foundation for project planning and bid-­
ding. The consequences of inadequate budgets and plans can be more
severe; that is, being overly optimistic can result in notable losses while
being overly pessimistic can lead to the loss of business possibilities.

In addition to being helpful for project yield analysis, cost and time
estimations are also important for project completion throughout the
development phase. Accurate project estimates are essential for the SP to
be administered properly. The PM(Person Month) should foresee any
potential issues and provide an appropriate fix. Estimating the time and
resources required is another important task for the project manager.
The SP manager needs to sketch out the sensitive success factors that

drive the project's design and administration. Avoiding project failure
requires it to overcome the limitations of developing the SP. The soft-­
ware engineering factors, which are controlled by the precise EE(Effort
Estimation) of the program, must carry out the SD team execution
process and resource allocation. Inconsistencies in the execution process
are also corrected by the PM. To accomplish the requirements for that
particular assignment, the PM applies the necessary methodologies
while accounting for the estimated effort. The success of the SP would
benefit from the use of project records. Furthermore, the estimation can
be performed in a somewhat reliable manner.

EE plays a crucial role in SPM. There are some serious problems as a
result of the incorrect development effort estimation. Software firms are
under serious pressure to deliver the highest-quality product within the
allotted time and financial constraints in today's competitive environ-­
ment [1]. If the development effort is undervalued, it will impair the
company's generosity and competitiveness; if it is overvalued, it will
result in a less-than-optimal use of valuable human resources, which will
reduce cost-effectiveness. By estimating, it is possible to estimate the SP
effort's most precise size, such as the number of months needed to build
software, or the number of resources required to finish the project on
schedule. In the end, it is converted to money [2]. The crucial aspects of
effort estimation are mentioned in Fig. 1.

The most challenging problem facing the software industry is still the
less effective management of SD budget predictions. Due to this, various
aspects (such as incorrect requirement engineering, unclear resource
elicitation, uncertain cost, and EE) must now be addressed by modern
SD organizations. These factors ultimately cause the development pro-­
cess to fail. To deal with these problems that cause chaos, the SD en-­
terprise must act as its anticipated aspect and create a counter
mechanism. Creating an early estimate of the entire process and deter-­
mining whether the resulting project can be implemented using only the
resources at hand are effective ways to address this problem. SEE cal-­
culates the amount of time required to accomplish the SD project or
procedure. The EE is crucial in the process of determining how much of
the relevant value of software is produced. SDEE is the process of
calculating the most realistic amount of labor per person-month
required to develop or maintain unfinished software based on inputs
like FP, size, software needs, UCP, and other factors [3]. The EE is also


used as input for the iteration plan, investment analysis, budgets, project
plan, pricing processes, and bidding rounds. The research has primarily
concentrated on developing formal SEE models or merely considering
UC or FP for the estimation of size or development effort, but it hasn't
taken the SRS of the programmed into account for such calculations [4].
As a result, it is necessary to develop a method that can estimate the SD
effort due to the proposed software's requirement-centered complexity

[5]. SEE models are split into two major categories. i) algorithmic and ii)
non-algorithmic. The former methods utilize a formula to estimate the
SC, for instance, COCOMO and FP. Conversely, the latter one doesn’t
utilize a formula for estimation, for instance, an analogy method.
Analogy methods estimate by comparing the fundamental facets of the
new project with the preceding finished one. This can also be applied to
projects that require just modifying the existing software to satisfy new
needs. For the precise estimation of the SC, the selection of a suitable
method and factor is important. Therefore, the SC as well as the project
profile, as of every chief factor encompassing project factors, customer
factors, software factors as well and team factors were studied and
analyzed. Algorithmic Model: This provides some mathematical for-­
mulas for Software estimation that are based on research and historical
data and makes use of inputs like the number of functions to be per-­
formed, the quantity of Source Lines of Code (SLOC) as well as other
Cost-Drivers (CD) such as skill levels, risk assessments, design approach,
language, etc. Many algorithmic models, including COCOMO models,
the Putnam model, and FP centred models, were developed. These
models are required as inputs because they provide accurate estimations
of certain factors, such as line of code (LOC), intricacy, and other factors,
which are challenging to ascertain in the early stages of an SD project.
One of the algorithmic schemes that Boehm starts is COCOMO. To
calculate the schedule, size, effort, and duration, COCOMO is used. The
three models that make up COCOMO are the Fundamental, Transitional,
and In-depth Models. Basic COCOMO calculates the effort for an SP that
ranges from smaller to medium that kind quickly and haphazardly. In-­
termediate and detailed COCOMO approaches to alter the code size into
the project in one month and at the most duration in a month. NonAlgorithmic models: During the early '90 s, this model was developed
for projecting cost estimation. Researchers have concentrated on
different approaches, which are centered upon soft computing

methodology, for instance, artificial neural networks, fuzzy logic models
along with genetic algorithms-centered implementations. Neural Net-­

related to the prediction of effort are mentioned in Fig. 2. This work

–
proposes a hybrid fusion based effort estimation framework that sys-­
tematically combines linear regression, decision tree, and random forest
models with hyperparameter optimization to improve prediction accu-­
racy. Unlike prior studies that rely on a single dataset or environment,
this study explicitly analyzes the impact of dataset diversity by vali-­
dating the model across multiple repositories such as China,
COCOMO81, PROMISE, and Kaggle. The proposed approach addresses
the poor generalization of existing models when tested on unseen
datasets. Additionally, comprehensive evaluation using multiple error
metrics (MAE, RMSE, MMRE, PRED, and R [2] ) provides a more robust
performance assessment than most earlier works. The integration of
model fusion with optimized learning distinguishes this study from

–
traditional standalone and expert judgment based estimation tech-­
niques. In this article, a detailed description for literature survey is
discussed with the help of tables in section-2. Research methodology and
implementation is done in section 3 and section 4. The result discussion
is discussed in detail in section 5. The subsequent section, section 6 and
section 7 contain conclusion and future scope.

**2. Literature review**

Over time, approaches for estimating software development efforts
have evolved, from traditional methods like function point analysis and


COCOMO to Machine Learning (ML) methods including ensemble
methods, decision trees, and linear regression. Accuracy is increased via
model fusion, and choosing and creating the appropriate characteristics
is crucial. Even yet, problems with project dynamics and data quality
necessitate ongoing improvement and adjustment of effort estimate
models. Table 1 mentions the comprehensive survey of the literature.

–
The year wise since (2010 2023) bibliographic representation of
effort estimation is graphically represented in Fig. 3. This includes an
article related to the computation of effort with traditional techniques
like function point, COCOMO model and expert judgment method. In
addition to this, it also utilizes computation of effort using various ML
techniques.

**3. Research methodology**

The methodology of the suggested work entails the study of different
ML techniques from their complexity and accuracy point of view. For
estimating the effort necessary for a software product, various meth-­
odologies will be employed. The impact of various data sets as well as
various surroundings will be investigated. The actual data related to
software projects will be accessed from Kaggle, COCOMO81, Promise
data Repository, and other repositories. The process of software esti-­
mation is to accurately predict the effort required to develop a software
product. The models already developed give good results, only for
projects, which are similar to one used for training the model and their
results deviate when tested using different data sets. The motive of this
work is to analyze the effect of using diverse data sets on software

estimation models. Project managers have traditionally found it difficult
to estimate effort. Numerous researchers have made various sorts of

*3.1. Effort estimation using machine learning hybrid approach*

In SD, the EE is important for the customers and developers.
Underestimating the effort may pave the way for the management to
approve the systems that could go beyond their budgets, with poorly
developed functions in addition to deprived quality. This may finally
lead to failure in task completion in the pre-set time frame. In all
computer-centric systems, the software is considered as the heart of the
system. This vital part is developed with proper guidelines. The top
priority for every firm is to produce software solutions efficiently. The
correct calculation of the effort required to complete the projects is the
main objective. Numerous studies have demonstrated that projects often
end up costing more than expected and taking longer to complete than
anticipated. In an SD process, effective EE is the most alarming activity
in modern computing. Here, a new framework is proposed for the EE.


The EE is done utilizing a hybrid fusion based approach. The utilization
of the fusion approach helps in estimating the efforts of the software
with less cost and failure rates. The proposed approach is employed
together with optimization to attain an enhanced outcome. The opti-­
mization process is done while utilizing the linear regression, decision
tree and random forest ML algorithms which aids in the improved per-­
formance of the model. Various parameters like RE, MRE, MMRE, Mean
Absolute Relatives Error (MARE), and also Percentage of Prediction
(PRED) are calculated to screen the performance of the model, and the
resulting effort is compared with various existing models to confirm the
proposed system efficiency. The proposed system could be elucidated
further using the block diagram.

*3.1.1. Dataset description*

The given dataset contains information about various software
development projects. Here is a description of the columns in the dataset
[(https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/gpreda/chinese-mnist): Depending](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/gpreda/chinese-mnist)
on the application, there are vast variations in the datasets used in ML,
particularly for the Random Forest, Linear Regression and Decision Tree
algorithms. For example, a dataset may contain attributes like location,
number of bedrooms, and square footage when predicting home values.
As an ensemble approach, Random Forest gains from a variety of data-­
sets covering various facets of the issue. For datasets where there is an


5

*Ritu et al.* *Egyptian* *Informatics* *Journal* *33* *(2026)* *100914*


approximately linear connection between the independent and depen-­
dent variables, linear regression is a helpful approach. This makes it
suitable for uses like using previous data to anticipate stock prices.
Because decision trees are versatile in processing both numerical and
categorical data, they are effective in datasets with complicated decision
boundaries, such as those that categorise medical illnesses based on
multiple symptoms. The datasets that are used in the healthcare sector
for ML applications vary according to the specific job that is being
performed. For example, a dataset may include demographics, medical
history, and other health markers to forecast how a disease would

progress.

Because Random Forest can handle complex relationships and highdimensional data, it performs well in scenarios such as these. To ascer-­
tain the linear association between variables like age, cholesterol, and
heart disease risk, one can do linear regression analysis on datasets.
Decision trees are often employed in healthcare datasets to identify risk
factors for conditions since they are interpretable and capable of
handling a wide range of data types. The datasets' richness and rele-­
vance, which mirror the intricacy of the real-world issues these algo-­
rithms are meant to solve, are ultimately what determine how successful
these algorithms will be. The datasets utilised by ML systems in the
healthcare industry differ based on the task being carried out.

To predict how an illness might proceed, for instance, a dataset may
contain demographics, medical history, and other health indicators.
Random Forest works effectively in situations like this because it can
handle high-dimensional data and intricate interactions. One may do
linear regression analysis on datasets to determine the linear connection
between variables such as age, cholesterol, and heart disease risk. De-­
cision trees are often employed in healthcare datasets to identify risk
factors for particular conditions since they are interpretable and capable
of handlang a wide range of data types. The description of all the used
attributes from the dataset is elaborated in Table 2.

The dataset appears to contain information about multiple software
development projects, including details such as the size of the project,
the number of inputs/outputs/interfaces, lines of code added/changed/
deleted, resource allocation, duration, development type, and effort

estimation.

*3.2. Machine learning*

Within artificial intelligence (AI), ML is a revolutionary field that is
changing how computers analyze information and make judgments.
Fundamentally, ML enables computers to recognize patterns in data,
learn from them, and adapt without the need for explicit programming.

**Table 2**

Description of the attribute used from the China dataset.

Attributes Description

measure the size and complexity of a software application.

application.

process.

development process.
Deleted Represents the number of lines of code deleted or removed during the
development process.
Resource Indicates the number of resources or individuals assigned to the project.
Duration Represents the duration or time taken to complete the project.
DevType Indicates the type of development, whether it is a new development or
maintenance of an existing application.
AdjFactor This represents an adjustment factor applied to the effort estimation.
Effort Indicates the effort or work required to complete the project.


The foundation of this field is made up of three elements: data, algo-­
rithms, and models. The cornerstone, data, is the source of insights and,
because of its superior quality, has a major effect on how successful
models are. The workhorses of computing are the three groups of al-­
gorithms: supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning para-­
digms. In supervised learning, models that map inputs to outputs are
trained using labelled datasets. Reinforcement learning, on the other
hand, makes use of environmental interaction to guide agents towards
the optimal decisions, whereas unsupervised learning analyses unla-­
belled data to discover underlying structures. The finished output,
models, capture learnt patterns to enable predictions on new data.
Models range from complicated NN to decision trees, and they are
available in various levels of complexity to meet a variety of needs.

The field of ML is rife with challenges and ethical quandaries.
Because faulty or biased datasets can distort model findings, data quality
is essential. It may be challenging to comprehend decision-making
processes when evaluating complex models, which are commonly
referred to as “black boxes,” especially in crucial industries like
healthcare. Ethical issues arise when biases in ML outcomes are inad-­
vertently amplified. Finding the right balance between model accuracy
and fairness requires ongoing effort. Computational resources are
another crucial component; deep learning models with high resource
requirements might be challenging for smaller organisations to deploy.
However, a variety of businesses are using ML, showcasing its revolu-­
tionary potential.


*3.2.1. Linear regression algorithm*

A fundamental approach in statistics and ML, linear regression pos-­
tulates a linear connection to explain the relationship between an output
and one or more inputs. The coefficients and the bias term that char-­
acterize this line establish the model's parameters. The linear regression
algorithm works simply. Initially, a hypothesis function is constructed,
and parameters are initialized, frequently at random. The algorithm
then uses an optimization approach, usually gradient descent, to itera-­
tively alter the parameters to minimize a cost function. Better model fit
is indicated by lower values. Regularization techniques penalize com-­
plex models, hence preventing overfitting. There are several fields in
which linear regression is used, including as biology, engineering, eco-­
nomics, and finance. Because of its simplicity and ease of interpretation,
it is advised for use as a baseline model and for preliminary study. It
might not be appropriate, nonetheless, for datasets with non-linear
patterns or extremely complex interactions. The performance of linear
regression algorithm w.r.t the China dataset is shown in Fig. 9.

It's critical to remember that linear regression presupposes a linear
connection between the target variable and the input data. The best
approach might not be linear regression if the connection is non-linear,
and more complex regression models, such as polynomial regression or
nonlinear regression, might be required. Additionally, there are varia-­
tions of linear regression, such as multiple linear regression (when there


ML has a wide range of applications. In the medical profession, it aids
in illness diagnosis, medication development, and treatment planning.
ML based demand forecasting, inventory control, and customized mar-­
keting are advantageous for retail. It is essential to the development of
autonomous vehicles in the automobile sector because it improves
perception, navigation, and decision-making.

Several factors are reshaping the ML field as we look to the future.
Explainable AI (XAI) is becoming more and more popular as a solution to
the interpretability problem since it makes model decision-making
processes transparent. Federated learning is a decentralized model
training technique that protects privacy by storing raw data locally on
devices. By combining edge computing with ML, models can run directly
on devices, eliminating the need for continuous data transfer to
centralized servers. Research on continuous learning is still in progress,
to enable models to adjust to new data without losing track of previously
learned information. The AI community is placing more emphasis on
ML's ethical aspects, such as bias reduction and justice.

Step-1. Input Data: Represents the input data X (independent variables) and Y
(dependent variable).
Step-2. Initialize Parameters: Initializes the parameters θ0,θ1,…,θn randomly or with
predefined values.
Step-3. Hypothesis Function: Represents the linear relationship between input
features and the predicted output.
Step-4. Calculate Cost: Computes the cost function J(θ) using the mean squared error.
Step-5. Verifies whether the algorithm has converged via a convergence check. If the
process converges, it is over. Go on to the following stages if convergence is not

achieved.

Step-6. Gradient Descent: This step applies the gradient descent technique to update

parameters.
Step-7. Update the settings according to the gradient descent step
Step-8. Loop Back: For the subsequent iteration, returns to the Hypothesis Function.
Step-9. Training Complete: Signifies that the training period has come to a close.
Step-10. Prediction: Makes predictions on fresh data using the trained model.


*3.2.2. Random forest algorithm*

An ensemble learning approach called Random Forest combines
many decision trees to produce a prediction model that is more reliable
and accurate. It is applicable to jobs involving both classification and
regression. Here's a detailed explanation of the Random Forest algo-­
rithm along with a diagram: To build a Random Forest model, first
gather a dataset including the input features and the matching output
variable. Then carefully prepare the data by removing missing values,
removing outliers, and performing any necessary normalization or
transformations. A decision tree ensemble is constructed using a
Random Forest, which effectively mitigates overfitting by training each
tree on a random fraction of the data and features. The use of


**Fig. 5.** Working Architecture of Random Forest Algorithm.

8

*Ritu et al.* *Egyptian* *Informatics* *Journal* *33* *(2026)* *100914*


bootstrapping, which generates numerous training sets by randomly
sampling the dataset with replacement, and random feature selection at
decision tree nodes are noteworthy techniques used to improve the
model variety and lower inter-tree correlation. Building decision trees in
the forest requires splitting points and features through recursive opti-­
mization based on Gini impurity or information gain. Post-construction,
predictions are made for each tree, and for classification tasks, the ma-­
jority voting principle is applied, while regression tasks utilize aver-­
aging. Metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score (for
classification), mean squared error, and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) (for
regression) are used to thoroughly assess the model's performance.

The general idea can be represented as follows in Eq. (2):


*F* ( *X* ) [1]
*N*

where:


*N*

*f* *i* ( *X* ) (2)


uncertainty or impurity in the data, such as information gain or Gini
impurity. Part of the structure of a decision tree is the algorithm's ability
to make intelligent choices at each branching point. The essential parts
of the decision tree are the internal and leaf nodes.

Each internal node represents a decision based on a particular
feature, acting as a gatekeeper to guide the traversal of the tree. On the
other hand, leaf nodes, which stand for the destination of a journey, are
associated with class labels in classification tasks or numerical values in
regression tasks. Decision trees provide itself to easy interpretation, so
practitioners may learn how the model makes decisions.

The splitting criteria, which comprise information gain and Gini
impurity, are the primary factors that guide the algorithm's decisions
throughout the building of the decision tree. These criteria are crucial
for determining the best feature and split point for each internal node in
order to appropriately capture patterns and relationships within the
data. Recursion is one characteristic that distinguishes the decision treebuilding approach.

The algorithm repeatedly divides the input into subsets at each in-­
ternal node, creating a structure that captures ever-more-specific pat-­
terns. This recursive process continues until a halting criteria is met. The
halting condition can be set to a maximum tree depth, a minimum
number of samples at a leaf node, or other predefined conditions. This
deliberate stopping helps to maintain a fair trade-off between general-­
isation and model complexity by preventing overfitting. The decision
tree's last phase is prediction. Predictions are formed by going from the
root node to the leaf node of the tree and based on the values of the input
characteristics.

Whereas regression tasks produce a numerical value associated with
the leaf node as the projected output, classification tasks use the class
label linked with the leaf node as the predicted class. This final step in
the decision tree's creation turns it into an effective tool that can make

defensible predictions based on discovered patterns in the data.


F(x) is the final prediction,
N is the number of trees in the forest,
f i (x)is the prediction of the \(i\)-th tree.
Each tree is built independently, and the randomness in both data
and features helps to decorate the trees and improve the overall per-­
formance of the model. Although there are just two decision trees in the
Random Forest illustration, a Random Forest usually has more than two
decision trees. Every tree undergoes separate training using a different
subset of the training set, and each tree's predictions are generated
uniquely. The average (regression) or majority vote (classification) of
each individual tree forecast determines the final prediction. When
managing noisy or missing data, capturing non-linear correlations, and
handling high-dimensional data, Random Forests work well. Addition-­
ally, they offer you insights on feature significance, which let you know
how significant each feature is in relation to the others throughout the
prediction process.

*3.2.3. Decision tree algorithm*

Regression and classification problems are two applications for the
supervised learning technique known as the Decision Tree algorithm.
With the properties of the incoming data, it builds a tree-like model of
decisions and their potential outcomes. Building a decision tree for ML
requires several basic processes, all of which are essential to converting
unprocessed data into a predictive model. The process begins with data
collection, which assembles a large dataset consisting of the related
output variable, also called the dependent variable or goal, and input
characteristics, also called independent variables. The previously
described dataset serves as the foundation for the subsequent stages of
the decision tree construction process. The process continues with data
preparation, which is a crucial step that includes cleaning the data and
ensuring it's ready for analysis, once it has been gathered. This stage
includes handling outliers, managing missing values, and performing
any necessary data transformations or normalisation processes. Through
careful preparation of the dataset, practitioners provide the foundation
for a dependable and strong decision tree model.

The decision tree construction procedure revolves around the tree
creation phase. Now, the decision tree algorithm begins its recursive
journey by carefully segmenting the data into subgroups based on the
input feature values. Each node's data must be partitioned using an
optimal characteristic selected by the algorithm. This decision is sup-­
ported by assessment measures that measure how well a split decreases


This represents a simplified decision tree with three classes and three
features. The conditions in each case are based on comparing the fea-­
tures to certain thresholds.

The decision tree in the diagram is created by repeatedly dividing the
data according to several criteria and thresholds. Every leaf node rep-­
resents a class label or a numerical value, and every interior node re-­
flects a judgment based on a particular characteristic. The Working
Architecture for the Decision Tree algorithm is mentioned in Fig. 6. The
tree starts with a root node that asks a question about Feature A. If the
answer is “yes” (Feature A *<* 5), the tree moves to the left and assigns
Class 1. If the answer is “no,” the tree moves to the right and asks another
question about Feature B. The process continues until a leaf node is
reached, and the corresponding class or value is assigned as the pre-­
diction. Decision trees can handle categorical and numerical informa-­
tion and are interpretable. They are susceptible to overfitting, though,
particularly if the tree gets too big. Methods like pruning and setting
appropriate stopping criteria can help mitigate overfitting and improve
generalization.

*3.2.4. Spatial Arrangement*

The size of an output volume is regulated by the 3 hyper-parameters
like depth, stride and zero-padding.

Depth is a hyperparameter of an output volume. It refers to the

*Ritu et al.* *Egyptian* *Informatics* *Journal* *33* *(2026)* *100914*

are described by variables that are generated and internally learned
from the dataset that is presented. These are referred to as model pa-­
rameters, and we have no control over how they vary as they rely on the
kind of data. 'M' and 'C' in a linear equation, for example, represent the
coefficient values found in the given dataset. Hyperparameters are the
name for a collection of adjustable parameters that control how an al-­
gorithm or model behaves and result in an optimized model with
optimal performance. The one-word response for Hyperparameters is
Configuration. “Train-Test Split Ratio (80–20)” is the hyperparameter
for our model of straightforward linear regression.

*3.2.6. Hyperparameter space*

For every selected algorithm(s), there is a list of HPs; our task is to
identify the ideal combination of HPs and to get the best outcomes by
carefully modifying them. We will be able to reach the Hyperparameter
Space by this technique, and this combination will surely produce the
finest optimum outcomes; but locating this combination will need
scanning the whole space. In this context, any possible combination of
the selected HP value is called a “MODEL,” and it needs to be assessed
right away. GridSearch CV and RandomSearch CV are two general

“crossmethods for efficiently exploring the HP space as a result. Here,
validation” (CV) is used.

one pixel at a time if the stride value is high. The filters leap two pixels at
a time as they are moved around if the stride equals two (or, in excep-­
tional cases, three or more). This would generate spatially small output
volumes.

its border. It stands as a hyperparameter concerning its size. Its feature is
that it would permit control of the spatial output size. It would be uti-­
lized to precisely maintain the spatial size of an input volume hence the
input's and output's w and h are the same.

*3.2.5. Hyper-parameter tuning*

The process of modifying the model's parameters, known as hyper-­
parameter tuning, is essentially a drawn-out one. Understanding the
importance of “Hyperparameter Tuning (HPs-T)” is essential for every
ML engineer and data scientist when selecting the optimal deep learning
or ML model and optimizing the model's performance (s).

Make it simple, as selecting the right collection of hyperparameters is
the only thing that may make selecting a ML model a challenging
endeavor. For a model to be trained, each of these is required. Ulti-­
mately, better hyperparameter tweaking and selection strategies lead to
an improvement in the ML model's performance. It always refers to the
chosen model's parameters, which you should always remember are
required before the model moves on to the training phase and cannot be
inferred from the data. Predictions, classification, and other operations


*3.2.7. Steps to perform hyperparameter tuning*

1. Choose the appropriate class of model.
2. Review the model's parameter list and create the HP space.
3. Identifying the techniques for hyperparameter space search
4. Utilizing a cross-validation methodology

To evaluate the model, calculate the model score.
**Train Test Split Estimator-** The test and train size for the given
dataset are set using permutations, which, when combined with the
random state, produce the same set of splits. If this step is skipped, a
different set of test and train sets will be produced, making it difficult to
trace your model's behavior during evaluation. To stabilize the model,
the random number generator receives its seed from the random state.
The two most effective ways to tune hyperparameters are as follows:

 - GridSearchCV

 - RandomisedSearchCV

*3.2.7.1. GridSearchCV.* The GridSearchCV method is used to evaluate
the artificial intelligence model for various hyperparameter settings.
This method is termed GridSearchCV because it looks at a grid of
hyperparameter values to find the optimal set of hyperparameters. As-­
sume, for instance, that we wish to select two distinct sets of values for
the Logistic Regression Classifier model's hyperparameters, C and Alpha.
The grid search method will be used to build the ideal model using a
variety of different hyperparameter combinations.

*3.2.7.2. RandomisedSearchCV.* GridSearchCV has limitations because it
only considers a finite set of hyperparameter parameters. Random-­
izedSearchCV addresses these limitations. It wanders randomly around
the grid in search of the perfect set of hyperparameters. This method gets
rid of unnecessary calculations.

**4. Implementation**

To increase the precision and dependability of effort estimates in
software development or project management, a hybrid fusion strategy
that uses ML to forecast effort often combines many predictive models or
approaches. The practice of projecting how much money and resources
are needed to finish a development project is called effort estimation.


10

*Ritu et al.* *Egyptian* *Informatics* *Journal* *33* *(2026)* *100914*

**Fig. 7.** Proposed Methodology.


Increasing the precision of estimations for software development pro-­
jects is the aim of this study. To do this, a system will be developed and
applied to accessible datasets utilizing a range of machine-learning
techniques. In this paper, we suggest boosting as a method to improve
software development project effort estimation accuracy. By fitting
several models, each with a low error rate, and then merging them into
an ensemble that could perform better, the process known as “boosting”
can raise the accuracy of any learning system.

Many algorithms have been used to estimate effort which ranges
from linear regression, decision tree, and random forest algorithm.
Here's a general outline in Fig. 7 of how fusion approach will work. Mean
Squared Error (MSE): It seems to have been an apostrophe used after
“MSE”. MSE in statistics and ML does not have a standard notation called

“MSE'”. The average of the squared differences between the predicted
and actual values is known as the mean squared error, or MSE.

The formula for MSE is:

model's performance is the MAE. It calculates the mean absolute dif-­
ference between the expected and actual (observed) values. The
following is the formula for MAE:

Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): The Root Mean Squared Error, or
RMSE, is one statistic used to evaluate the performance of a regression
model. In this variation, the square root is calculated in addition to the

the data, reprocessing techniques are used to handle missing values,
outliers, and inconsistencies. The feature selection and engineering step
next uses data analysis and domain experience to determine the most
critical project qualities, finding relevant features that impact work
estimation. The next step is algorithm selection, where a set of ML al-­
gorithms is chosen to model the effort prediction with an emphasis on
regression.

In addition to more complex techniques like gradient boosting or
NNs, these algorithms include support vector machines, decision trees,
random forests, and linear regression. In the individual model training
stage, each selected technique is trained using a subset of the historical
data by dividing the data into training and validation sets. Hyper-­
parameters are adjusted for optimal model performance. The process
then shifts to model fusion, where various methods of combining the
output of many models are examined. Taking into account are hybrid
models that integrate the best features of many algorithms and ensemble
approaches such as weighted or averaged averaging (e.g., a neural
network that mixes traditional data with outputs from other regression
models).

In testing and validation, regression metrics like as MAE and RMSE
are employed to evaluate the model's performance on an alternative test
dataset. This assessment also provides information on the forecast ac-­
curacy and ensures that the model may be used with fresh data. The
feedback loop offers a way to continuously monitor and update when
new project data becomes available. Retraining the model on a regular
basis helps it increase forecast accuracy over time and adapts to
changing project dynamics. Analysing forecast mistakes and seeking
advice from subject matter experts is part of the ongoing process of
iterative improvement, which aims to make the approach better.
Experimenting with different feature combinations, algorithms, and
fusion techniques can assist to increase accuracy.

This comprehensive method demonstrates how project effort esti-­
mation is dynamic and necessitates ongoing improvement.

Through the integration of ML methodologies and domain knowl-­
edge, this approach aims to create resilient and flexible models for
project effort prediction that accurately reflect the dynamic nature of
software development projects. Subheadings can be used to break up
each part. It should give a clear and simple explanation of the experi-­
mental findings, their meaning, and any inferred experimental
implications.

strength and direction of linear relationships between pairs of columns
in the data frame. Stronger positive correlations are shown by warmer
hues, stronger negative correlations by cooler hues, and little to no as-­
sociation is indicated by values near zero. To give more quantitative
details regarding the interactions between variables, the numeric cor-­
relation coefficients are also shown in the heatmap's cells. To determine
the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for every feature in a data frame, a
function called mulcol is built. Regression model multicollinearity is
found using VIF. “Features” and “VIF” will be the two columns in a data
frame that is formed. It computes the VIF using the variance inflation
factor function from stats models for each column in the standardized
array arr. In the final data frame, rows are created using the VIF values
and accompanying feature names. Using the variance inflation factor
function, the nested list comprehension iterates through each column in
the standardized array to determine the VIF. The feature name (obtained
from x.columns[col]) and its related VIF value are contained in the inner
list [x.columns[col], variance inflation factor(arr, col)]. Using range(arr.
shape[6]), the outer list comprehension loops through each column
index in the standardized array. Two columns are present in the
generated Data Frame: “Features” and “VIF”. The names of the charac-­
teristics are listed in the “Features” column, and the corresponding VIF
values are listed in the “VIF” column. computes the maximum scores
after that.

**Fig. 11.** Representation of the analysis of the resultant score graphical form.

model, most likely a decision tree or a random forest, using a grid search
technique. This grid search will be used to find the best combination of
hyperparameters for the model. Representation of the analysis of the
resultant score in graphical form is shown in Fig. 11. Here the following
parameters are used to get the best result. 'criterion': This is a hyper-­
parameter that specifies the criterion used to measure the quality of a
split in a decision tree or random forest. The code is considering four
different criteria: “squared error,” “absolute error,” “poison,” and “en-­
tropy.” These show many metrics for assessing a split's quality. “max
depth”: The decision tree's maximum depth is managed by this hyper-­
parameter. It is configured to be an inclusive range from 2 to 19,
meaning that for hyperparameter tweaking, the code will experiment
with various tree depths between 2 and 19. “max features”: This
hyperparameter regulates how many features are taken into account in a
decision tree or random forest split. The typical choices for this


hyperparameter, “auto” and “log2,” are taken into consideration by the
code. Using “log2 ″ means taking the number of characteristics and
squaring it with the base-2 logarithm; using ”auto“ means taking
advantage of every attribute. Leaf sample, min. This hyperparameter
specifies the minimum number of samples required at a leaf node. The
code will experiment with different numbers since it is programmed to
range from 1 to 9 in order to find the minimum number of samples
required at each leaf node. The absolute minimal number of samples
required to divide an internal node is indicated by the hyperparameter
”min samples split“. The code will experiment with different values for
the minimum number of samples required to split a node, with its range
set at 2 to 9. Estimators 'n': This hyperparameter controls the number of
trees in the forest.Fig. 12..

There are four different values for the number of trees in the random

forest that the algorithm considers. When you execute a grid search
using this parameter grid, the software will systematically evaluate the
model's performance for every possible combination of these

hyperparameters. It will train and assess the model using crossvalidation or an alternative validation method for each combination.

determine which combination of hyperparameters yields the highest
performance on the selected evaluation measure, such as accuracy or
mean squared error. This procedure can assist in optimizing the model's
performance on the provided dataset. Fig. 11 illustrates the performance
metrics score in a graphical style. Table 6 displays the Metrics Error for
the suggested hybrid strategy.

state, training data shape(x), training data shape(y), test data shape(x),
test data shape(y), training score, and test score were different and were
inaccurate. After testing the China dataset the value is accurate and the
accuracy was changed.

understanding of the analysis that was conducted by using several

after analysis is shown in Fig. 14.

**6. Conclusion**

In conclusion, precise effort estimation continues to be a major dif-­
ficulty in the ever-changing field of software development. Over time,
initial projections become less trustworthy due to the inherent unpre-­
dictability in the software development process and changing customer
expectations. To improve effort estimate, this research study has pro-­
posed an approach that makes use of ensemble methods and ML,
particularly random forest algorithms and linear regression. Using a
fusion strategy, which combines predictions via stacking, has been a
crucial component of our process. This method offers a more precise and
reliable estimate of project work in addition to accommodating the
dynamic requirements of agile projects. We have made sure that our
results are reliable by training the model on a large dataset from the
China dataset repository. In addition, we have combined the output of


**Fig. 13.** Graphical representation of dataset view and analysis for testing and training before analysis.

15

*Ritu et al.* *Egyptian* *Informatics* *Journal* *33* *(2026)* *100914*

**Fig. 14.** Graphical representation of dataset view and analysis for testing and training after analysis.


the ensemble model with a linear regression model to further improve
the estimate procedure. This stage has allowed us to further validate the
efficacy of our strategy by allowing us to compare the efficiency of our
suggested model with specific regression models. In conclusion, it is
impossible to exaggerate the importance of accurate and reliable effort
assessment in software development. This research has shown that a
fusion strategy, which combines ensemble techniques with ML, has
potential to increase the accuracy of effort assessment at different phases
of the software development life cycle. These results open the door to
more trustworthy and knowledgeable decision-making in software
project management, which will eventually help software development
projects succeed.

**7. Future scope**

Future software development effort estimation might benefit from a
trajectory towards more flexibility, complexity, and ethical concerns
when ensemble ML techniques and fusion approaches are used. To in-­
crease accuracy and robustness, researchers and practitioners will likely
look into more complex ensemble approaches in the future. They will
likely go beyond conventional models and employ cutting-edge tech-­

—
niques. Hybrid models which fuse ML with other strategies like rule
—
based systems or expert opinion may emerge. Moreover, there is a
growing emphasis on improving model interpretability and incorpo-­
rating domain-specific knowledge to ensure that effort estimation
closely aligns with the nuances of various organisations. It is possible
that in the future, dynamic models that adjust instantly to the dynamics
of projects and continuous learning processes that improve forecasts
based on continuous input will be developed. The focus will shift to
addressing biases and guaranteeing fair and equitable predictions as
ethical concerns become more prominent. Other trends that should be
expected are the combination of effort estimation models with DevOps
practices, benchmarking standards, and international cooperation for
data sharing. Additionally, areas that might see more attention include
estimating the impact of technical debt and taking forecast uncertainties
into account. Essentially, a comprehensive and cooperative approach
that prioritizes ongoing development, moral issues, and the incorpora-­
tion of new technologies characterizes the future of effort estimation in
software development.
